profiles.meeting_scenario: A hospital-affiliated community health research center is holding a design review of a draft author checklist and manuscript template based on the TREND statement for investigators submitting nonrandomized evaluations of behavioral and public health interventions. The template is intended for an upcoming internal pilot across three projects already in development: a pharmacist-led hypertension coaching program in community clinics, a school-based vaping prevention initiative, and a county diabetes self-management outreach program. In this meeting, the participants are reviewing whether the current draft is ready for pilot rollout, whether the prompts are framed clearly enough to elicit TREND-relevant reporting, and what light edits should be made before circulation. The expected outcome is a decision to approve the draft for a limited pilot with a short list of wording changes and one final methods pass.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.expertise: Nonrandomized intervention evaluation, implementation science, reporting standardization
members.background: A PhD-trained public health methodologist who oversees evaluation design support for community and clinic-based intervention studies and has previously led center-wide adoption of common reporting templates.
members.private_state: She wants the template approved quickly so teams can start using it before the next submission cycle, and she is trying to balance methodological completeness with a form that busy investigators will actually finish.
hidden_assumptions: When a reporting template asks for the study's 'theory,' investigators can satisfy that by giving a concise logic model, program rationale, or mechanism narrative even if they do not name a formal theory.

A prompt for the 'comparison condition' should capture what participants would otherwise have experienced in practice, including routine counseling, school programming, or standard services that form the practical counterfactual.

A section for 'bias adjustment methods' can be a single compact narrative field that covers major design and analysis steps without requiring structured subfields for diagnostics or implementation details.
A draft is 'ready for pilot' once it is coherent and usable enough to test with real investigators, even if the wording still needs tightening after initial submissions.

members.name: Dr. Nathan Cho
members.role: Clinical Epidemiologist and Methods Review Lead
members.expertise: Evidence synthesis, quasi-experimental methods, reporting guideline interpretation
members.background: An MD-MPH epidemiologist who advises journal authors on nonrandomized study reporting and regularly extracts study details for systematic reviews of public health interventions.
members.private_state: He wants the center's template to be rigorous enough that downstream reviewers can appraise studies without chasing missing details, and he worries that a permissive pilot draft will normalize vague reporting habits.
hidden_assumptions: When a template asks for 'theory,' the expected response is a clearly identified theoretical or causal framework tied to intervention components, mediators, and outcome choice, not just a practical rationale.

A prompt labeled 'comparison condition' should refer to the defined condition or group used for comparison in the evaluation, while ambient services or background programming belong under setting or context instead.

A section for 'bias adjustment methods' should contain enough structure that authors report the actual adjustment approach in an appraisable way, including what was adjusted for and how the adjustment was implemented.
A draft is only 'ready for pilot' when the pilot tests uptake of a nearly publication-grade reporting standard rather than serving mainly as a usability exercise for a still-loose form.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss strengthening the template's prompt for the study's 'theory.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a short logic model, intervention rationale, or explanation of why the program should influence behavior or outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a named behavioral, social, or causal framework that can be mapped to components, mediators, and measured outcomes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In public health reporting conversations, 'theory' sounds like a settled methodological term, and both sincerely want stronger reporting here, so the shared word creates an easy false sense of alignment.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'comparison condition' prompt is supposed to capture
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the template needs a clear prompt for the 'comparison condition.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the prompt should draw out whatever participants would otherwise have received in the real world, including usual counseling, existing school health activities, or routine community services.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the prompt should only describe the actual study comparison group or condition, with surrounding background services documented elsewhere as context rather than as the comparison itself.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they are reviewing template wording rather than coding a specific paper, the phrase 'comparison condition' feels sufficiently precise on its face, and both view more complete prompting as obviously beneficial without noticing they are expanding different boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What a section for 'bias adjustment methods' should look like
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the template should include a section for 'bias adjustment methods.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 envisions one concise open-text section where investigators summarize how they addressed bias through design or analysis, such as matching, covariate adjustment, or site controls.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 envisions a more structured section with prompts or sub-items that make authors specify the adjustment method, variables addressed, and implementation details in a way a methods reviewer can assess.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At the design-review level, agreeing that a section should exist sounds like agreement on the requirement itself, while the disagreement is actually about the invisible mechanics of how much structure that section must impose.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss whether the draft is 'ready for pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means ready once investigators can start using it next month and generate practical feedback on missing or awkward prompts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ready only once the draft already encodes the core TREND expectations tightly enough that pilot use will not reinforce incomplete reporting norms.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'pilot' naturally implies an intermediate step, so both can sound equally supportive of moving forward while quietly applying different thresholds for what must be stable before that step.

turns.inner_thought: I need us to leave with a practical green light. The hypertension coaching, vaping prevention, and diabetes outreach teams are already moving, and if this stalls, we lose the next submission cycle. For me, ready for pilot means the draft is coherent enough that people can actually use it next month, and then we learn from where they hesitate or skip.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. What I'd like us to do today is decide whether this TREND-based checklist is ready for pilot across the three studies we already have in motion, and, if we're close, identify the smallest set of edits we need before it goes out.

turns.inner_thought: It is close, but I want the bar to stay high. If we send out a permissive draft, people will treat it as the center's standard, and then reviewers will still be chasing details. Ready for pilot should mean nearly stable and rigorous enough that someone extracting these studies later can appraise them without guessing.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. My impression is that it's close, so it may be most useful to focus on whether the current prompts will elicit reporting that's actually interpretable later for appraisal and synthesis.

turns.inner_thought: The theory prompt is where teams often freeze if it sounds too academic. I want them to feel they can give a short logic model, rationale, or mechanism narrative for why the intervention should change behavior or outcomes. If they can explain why each piece should matter, that's enough to start.
turns.utterance: One place I thought the revision helped was around the study's theory. As written now, it should do a better job of getting investigators to explain why the intervention components were expected to influence the outcomes they chose.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, but only if they identify the underlying theoretical or causal framework clearly enough to connect components, mediators, and endpoints. Otherwise they'll give a general rationale and reviewers will still have to infer the structure.
turns.utterance: I agree that's an important one. I wonder if we can tighten that prompt just a bit more so authors identify the theory clearly enough to link the components, the mediators, and the selected endpoints.

turns.inner_thought: And if we're trying to make these studies understandable, the comparison condition has to draw out the practical counterfactual—what people otherwise would have received in clinics, schools, or county services during that window. Teams underdescribe that unless you ask directly.
turns.utterance: Related to that, I think the comparison condition prompt needs to be very plain. It should push teams to spell out what participants were getting otherwise during the evaluation period.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the comparison condition should be the actual comparator in the evaluation, stated cleanly enough that a reviewer can see what intervention group is being compared against what condition. The surrounding services belong elsewhere, but I don't need to say that if we're aligned on clarity.
turns.utterance: Yes, I had the same reaction. A clearer comparison condition prompt would make it much easier for reviewers to see the intervention against the relevant comparison directly and consistently.

turns.inner_thought: The other high-value area is bias adjustment methods, but I have to protect usability. One compact narrative field is realistic; asking for too many boxes or method details will lose the clinic and community teams. I need enough to capture matching, covariate adjustment, site controls, and similar steps without making it feel like another methods section.
turns.utterance: The other area I'd still like in there is bias adjustment methods. I do think the template should include a section for that, but it needs to stay compact enough that the project teams will actually complete it.

turns.inner_thought: Compact is fine, but only if it's structured enough to be appraisable. They need to say what they adjusted for and how they implemented it, not just note that adjustment happened. A few prompts or cues would solve most of that without making the form huge.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think bias adjustment methods can still stay fairly lean if that section includes a few cues so authors indicate what they adjusted for and how they carried it through analytically.

turns.inner_thought: That's close enough for me to move. If we tighten those three spots, the form is usable and we'll learn quickly from real submissions. Pilot is the point where awkward wording shows up; I don't need every line polished to journal standard before anyone touches it.
turns.utterance: Right. With those wording refinements, the form feels ready for pilot to me, and I think we'd learn more from a first round of completed templates than from another long round of internal tweaking.

turns.inner_thought: I can go along with that if I get one more methods review before it circulates. I want to make sure the pilot version already supports consistent extraction of TREND elements, especially around adjustment and comparators. Pilot shouldn't mean loose.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. Before it circulates, I'd just want one final methods pass so the pilot version supports consistent extraction of the core TREND elements.

turns.inner_thought: Good—I'll summarize this as modest tightening, not expansion. Keep the form short, sharpen the prompts, and keep us on schedule. He can do his methods pass, and the teams can still get it in time.
turns.utterance: That's fine. So what I'm hearing is: tighten the theory prompt, clarify the comparison condition prompt, and use slightly stronger language in the bias adjustment methods section, but without really lengthening the form.

turns.inner_thought: Her summary sounds close enough to proceed, and I still assume those refinements will bring the draft up to a near publication-grade standard before the pilot goes out. If I review quickly, we can keep momentum without sacrificing rigor.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's a workable plan. Send me the revised draft once those small refinements are in, and I'll turn it around quickly so we can move toward pilot approval.
